content:
I think you might want to change the variable name of [[i]] because it gets used in the for loop as well.

Also, the goal should probably say '<<add>> the index value to [[sum]].' instead of 'from'.
Is it supposed to say 'if a letter has an even index' or is it referring to the [[i]] variable index?

I had to look at your solution to figure out, no way I would have guessed that the index you were referring to was the letter's original 0-based alphabetical index. Other than that, seems like a good puzzle.

[Goal]

- Please fix the add statement and the variable name "i", as suggested by @Sflubaduba.

- As @Sflubaduba has pointed out, the term "index" here is overloaded. You state that "If a number has an even index, add the index value from sum" but you solution only checks the 0-indexed index value of a letter (not the [[i]]-indexed index value your clash introduces). This creates some discrepancies in the clash; e.g. in the "Praise" test case, where using the [[i]]-indexed index values yields an answer of -603 instead of 603.

- Another thing I noticed in your solution: you divide sum by 2 on *each* iteration once all letters have been seen. This means that it is possible that division by 2 happens more than once, as seen in some of your cases. This is somewhat stated in your problem description "every time all the letters of the alphabet have been called" but this statement is unclear and can have multiple interpretations. It is better to make this rule explicit; one suggestion is to use bullet points to highlight that this rule is executed per letter seen.

[Constraints]

- Please move the last constraint to the Goal section.

- The test/validator case "Are we playing UNO?" violates the constraint 0 < n < 75. Please fix the case or update your constraints accordingly.

- It might be a good idea to limit the number of floating-point divisions required per test case.

[Cases]

- Please add more cases where [[i]] is more varied. There are too many cases where [[i]] is a small number like 0 or 1.

Thank you.

Just to add to @Sflubaduba's first comment,

* "[[i]] gets used in the for loop as well" refers to the variable name used in the for loop in the default code generated by the stub. That's why [[i]] should be changed to a different variable name so that it isn't overwritten. This is particularly important for players who want to use the default code without making significant changes to it.

* Both instances of "If a number" should be changed to "If a letter". "A" to "Z" are letters, not numbers.

As mentioned by both @Sflubaduba and @User123, the statement is confusing because it doesn't clearly distinguish between the indexes being used:

* deciding the operation (add or subtract) depends on the letter's 0-based index, whereas
* the index value actually being added or subtracted is the "i-based" index.

In addition to the excellent points already raised by @Sflubaduba and @User123, please also follow up on the following:

Goal
* [[sum]] is used but undefined. Please specify that its initial value is 0.

* Please change "[[i]] indexed" to "indexed starting at [[i]]" for clarity.

* Please specify that letter input should be treated in a case-insensitive manner.

Output
* Please specify that if the answer is an integer, it should be output without any decimal places; otherwise, it should be output with all decimal places and no trailing zeros.

Stub generator
* Please add a write statement, e.g. write answer.

Cases
* The uppercase letters K and W aren't used in any validators. Please modify the validators so that these letters are used in at least one validator.

* Please revise Validators 2 to 5 so that the input letters are more similar to those in their corresponding tests. For example, Test 2 uses a number of different lowercase letters, whereas Validator 2 uses only a few uppercase letters, so they aren't closely aligned.

* Please revise the cases so that each validator expects a similar *type* of output to its corresponding test, while the answers are still different. For example, both could expect small positive integers, or both could expect large negative floating-point values with three decimal places.

* There aren't any clear patterns in the case progression. Please order the case pairs according to some meaningful criteria.

Thanks.
